head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Alphabetical order: shorter prefixes come before the words that extend them, and ties of equal length are in alphabetical order
Set of words that can be built one letter at a time; the empty string seeds it
The word minus its last letter must already be buildable
Strict `>` keeps the alphabetically smaller word on ties, because words arrive in alphabetical order

p: `["a","banana","app","appl","ap","apply","apple"]` sorted:

blocks.h: Why must the list be sorted?
p: Without sorting, `appl` might be seen before `app` and rejected even though it becomes buildable later. Sorting guarantees every shorter prefix is decided before its extensions. `apple` and `apply` both have length 5; `apple` sorts first, becomes `best`, and the strict `>` stops `apply` from replacing it, so ties resolve to the alphabetically smaller word.

bullets: Time: O(n · L + n log n) for n words of length L.

720.takeaway: Sort, then keep a set of buildable words; a word is buildable if its prefix without the last letter is.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Cells to remove this round; a set avoids double counting cells that sit in both a row and a column match
Set union with the three cells of a match
board[i][j] = 0 for i, j in crush
Marks all crushed cells at once
Column compaction: keeps the surviving candies in order
Pads empties on top so survivors fall to the bottom
while True … if not crush: return
Repeat until the board is stable

blocks.h: Why mark first and remove afterwards?
p: All matches in a round happen at the same time. If cells were zeroed as soon as they were found, a later match that shares a cell (an L or T shape) would no longer see its candy and be missed. Collecting into a set first treats the round as one simultaneous event.

bullets: Time: O((m·n)²) worst case, since each round is O(m·n) and there can be O(m·n) rounds.
Space: O(m·n) for the crush set.

723.takeaway: Repeat: mark every horizontal/vertical triple at once, zero them, apply gravity per column, until nothing is marked.

What it does
Reach for it when

Insertion index found by binary search over tuples (compared lexicographically)
The previous booking ends after the new one starts: overlap
The next booking starts before the new one ends: overlap
Inserts at position i, O(n) shift

p: Bookings `10-20`, `15-25`, `20-30` (end times are exclusive):

blocks.h: Why only two neighbours need checking?
p: The list is sorted and has no overlaps. Any booking that could overlap the new one must be the closest one before or the closest one after the insertion point, because earlier bookings end even earlier and later ones start even later. Note `20-30` is accepted after `10-20` since intervals are half-open (end 20 does not collide with start 20).

bullets: Time: O(log n) to search, O(n) to insert.

729.takeaway: Keep bookings sorted, binary-search the slot, and compare only with the previous and next booking.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Asteroids that survive so far, in order
Chained comparison: a collision happens only when the new asteroid moves left and the top moves right
The top is smaller, so it explodes; check the next one
The `else` of a `while` runs when the loop ends WITHOUT `break`; the asteroid survives and is pushed

blocks.h: Why `while … else` and why a stack?
p: The new asteroid may destroy several in a row, so a loop is needed, and `break` signals that it was destroyed (or both were). If it exits normally, nothing is left to hit and it is pushed. The stack holds the right-moving asteroids that could still collide with future left-movers, and the most recent one collides first.

bullets: Time: O(n), each asteroid is pushed and popped at most once.

735.takeaway: Stack of survivors: a left-mover pops smaller right-movers; Python's while/else pushes it only if it was never stopped.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Index of the first letter strictly greater than target (binary search); `bisect_left` would stop at an equal letter
Next strictly greater element in a sorted list
Wraps around to index 0 when no letter is greater

p: The answer must be strictly greater than the target, so equal letters are skipped; `bisect_right` returns the position just after any equal ones. When the target is the largest letter (or bigger), the index equals `len(letters)`, and the modulo maps it back to 0, which implements the wrap-around rule.

744.takeaway: Binary search for the first element greater than the target (bisect_right), wrapping with modulo.

p: Only row pairs that share at least one column are shown:

Every rectangle has a top row and a bottom row. For a fixed pair, any two columns where both rows hold a 1 form its corners. Counting shared columns c and choosing 2 gives every rectangle for that pair exactly once.

bullets: Space: O(1). Iterating over the smaller dimension makes it faster.

750.takeaway: Fix a pair of rows, count columns where both have a 1, and add C(c, 2).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Maps a bottom pair (e.g. 'BC') to the letters allowed above it
Can a pyramid be completed from this row? A row of length 1 is done
Chooses a top letter for each adjacent pair, building the next row left to right (backtracking)
Remembers answers per row string, so the same row reached by different choices is not recomputed
Unknown pairs give an empty list, so that branch fails immediately

p: Bottom `BCD`, allowed `BCC, CDE, CEA, FFF`. The only complete next row built is:
bullets: `BC → C`, `CD → E` gives `CE`; then `CE → A` gives `A`: the pyramid completes, so the answer is True.

blocks.h: Why memoize on the row string?
p: Different choices for the top letters can produce the same next row. Caching `build(row)` ensures each distinct row is solved once, which keeps the search from exploding.

bullets: Time: exponential in the worst case (letters^length rows), reduced by caching and pruning.
Space: O(number of cached rows) plus recursion depth.

756.takeaway: Backtracking row by row (choose a top letter per adjacent pair), cached by row string.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Step number: both walkers have taken k steps, so walker at row i is at column k − i
Most cherries collected when walker 1 is in row i and walker 2 in row j after k steps
State = (i, j) because k fixes the columns
Each walker came from the left (same row) or from above (row − 1), giving four combinations
If both walkers stand on the same cell, count its cherry once
Thorns are impassable for either walker
If the end is unreachable the result stays at −inf, so return 0

p: `[[0,1,-1],[1,0,-1],[1,1,1]]`: the trip down and back is modelled as two walkers going down together. Rows show reachable states and the best count after each step:

head: step k
meaning
reachable states (i, j): cherries
best
rows: best per (row of walker 1, row of walker 2)
best per (row of walker 1, row of walker 2)
best per (row of walker 1, row of walker 2)
best per (row of walker 1, row of walker 2)

blocks.h: Why two walkers going forward instead of one going down and back?
p: The return trip, reversed, is another path from the start to the end. Two simultaneous walkers let the DP (Dynamic Programming) remember the shared cells (to avoid counting a cherry twice) with just their rows, because the step count fixes both columns. A one-way DP cannot know which cherries the first trip already took.

bullets: Time: O(n³): 2n steps times n² (i, j) pairs.
Space: O(n²) with the rolling `dp` layer.

741.takeaway: Cherry Pickup: two walkers move in lockstep down the grid, state (row1, row2) per step; same-cell cherries count once.

What it does
Reach for it when

Merging many sorted lists by sorting once
The latest end time among everything merged so far
The next interval starts after the busy period ended: a free gap [end, s]

p: Three employees; all intervals merged and sorted:

blocks.h: Why do gaps only appear between merged blocks?
p: Free time for everyone means no one is working. After sorting by start, if the next interval begins after the latest end seen so far, nobody is busy in between. If it begins earlier, someone is working, so no gap exists.

bullets: Time: O(N log N) for N intervals.

759.takeaway: Flatten, sort by start, and report the gaps between the running maximum end and the next start.

What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Where each person currently sits, so partners are found in O(1)
XOR (exclusive or) with 1 flips the lowest bit: 0↔1, 2↔3, 4↔5, which maps a person to their partner
The seat next to person i is wrong
Brings the partner next to person i; then both entries in `pos` are updated
Greedy fix, one couple per step
Each wrong pair costs exactly one swap here

head: seats
partner of left seat
action

swaps
rows: seat 1 should hold 1: swap with position 2

blocks.h: Why is fixing the left seat greedily optimal?
p: Each swap can fix at most one couple, and swapping the partner into place always fixes one without breaking anything already fixed. A group of k couples in a cycle needs k − 1 swaps, and the greedy uses exactly that. Equivalent: swaps = couples − number of cycles in the couple graph.

765.takeaway: XOR with 1 finds each partner; greedily swap the partner into the neighbouring seat, updating the position map.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Stack holding the MAXIMUM of each chunk so far; maxima are non-decreasing
x is smaller than the previous chunk's maximum, so x must be sorted into that chunk: the chunks merge
A merged chunk's maximum is the largest of the merged chunks

blocks.h: Why compare with `st[-1] > x` and not `>=`?
p: Equal values do not force a merge: `[4] [4]` can be sorted separately because the sorted order of two equal numbers is unchanged. A strict `>` leaves equal neighbours as separate chunks, which maximises the count. Using `>=` would merge them and lose chunks.

bullets: Time: O(n), each element is pushed and popped at most once.

768.takeaway: Monotonic stack of chunk maxima: a smaller incoming value merges all chunks with a larger maximum.

s in js for s in stones
A generator of booleans, one per stone
True counts as 1 and False as 0, so the sum counts the jewels

p: `jewels = "aA"`, `stones = "aAAbbbb"`:

blocks.h: Why a set rather than checking `s in jewels` on the string?
p: `s in jewels` on a string scans the characters, O(J) each, giving O(J·S) overall. A set makes each test O(1), so the total is O(J + S). For tiny inputs it does not matter, but the set is the habit to build.

771.takeaway: Put the jewels in a set, then count stones that are members (sum over booleans).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Forward there are two moves ((x, x+y) or (x+y, y)); backward there is only one, because the larger coordinate must have been produced by adding the smaller
Reversing a branching process into a deterministic one
Undoes many additions of ty at once (modulo instead of subtracting one at a time)
Cannot reduce ty further; tx can still shrink by multiples of ty, so check (tx − sx) is a multiple of ty
Final stretch handled in closed form

p: Start (1,1), target (3,5):

blocks.h: Why is modulo valid and not subtraction?
p: If tx is much bigger than ty, the last many moves all added ty to x, so repeated subtraction would be slow (up to 10⁹ steps). `tx %= ty` jumps straight to the remainder. The special case `ty == sy` prevents the modulo from overshooting below the start: the remainder could skip past sx.

bullets: Time: O(log max(tx, ty)), like the Euclidean algorithm.

780.takeaway: Reverse the process (only one predecessor exists) and speed it up with modulo, like Euclid's algorithm.

blocks.h: Why is this faster than testing each word separately?
p: Testing every word costs O(len(s)) each, O(len(s) · W) in total. Here `s` is scanned once and each word advances at most once per letter of the word, so the total work is O(len(s) + total letters in words).

bullets: Time: O(len(s) + sum of word lengths).
Space: O(number of words) for the waiting buckets.

792.takeaway: Scan s once; keep words in buckets keyed by the next letter they need and advance a word when its letter arrives.

Index of the latest element ≥ `left`; a valid subarray needs at least one such element
Number of valid subarrays ending at i: starts between bad + 1 and good
Counting subarrays by their right end

blocks.h: Why `good - bad` and not a count of window sizes?
p: For subarrays ending at i, any start after `bad` avoids too-large elements, and the start must be at or before `good` so the subarray contains an element ≥ left. The difference is never negative: whenever x > right, x is also ≥ left, so `bad` and `good` are both set to i and the count is 0 for that end.

795.takeaway: For each right end, valid starts lie in (bad, good]; count good − bad.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Minimum swaps so far if position i is NOT swapped
Minimum swaps so far if position i IS swapped (it counts the swap at i)
Both arrays are increasing without crossing: keep→keep, swap→swap
Crossing is increasing: keep→swap and swap→keep
Impossible transitions; both conditions together can both hold

blocks.h: Why can both conditions be true at once?
p: When both hold (e.g. values far apart), keeping or swapping the pair are both consistent with either previous state, so each new state takes the min over both transitions. The code applies the first condition first and then lets the second one improve it with `min`.

801.takeaway: Two-state DP (keep/swap) per index; valid transitions depend on whether neighbours stay increasing straight or crossed.

Comparing all pairs of people is O(n²) with n up to 20,000. Ages are bounded, so grouping reduces the work to O(distinct_ages²) ≈ O(120²), independent of n.

For a guess w, groups the remaining candidates by the score they would produce
Counting how a guess splits the candidates
The size of the biggest group: the worst case if w is guessed
Chooses the guess whose worst-case group is smallest
cand = [x for x in cand if match(best, x) == m]
Keeps only words consistent with the score the master returned

p: Words `acckzz, ccbazz, eiowzz, abcczz`, secret `abcczz` (the master is simulated by `match(guess, secret)`):

blocks.h: Why choose the guess that minimises the biggest group?
p: The feedback is a number of matching positions. A guess that splits the candidates into several small groups leaves few words whichever feedback comes back. Picking the minimax guess (smallest worst-case group) makes the candidate list shrink fast enough to finish within 10 guesses.

bullets: Time: O(10 · N² · L): each round compares every candidate pair, with N words of length L (6).

843.takeaway: Minimax guessing: pick the word whose worst feedback group is smallest, then filter candidates by the returned score.

What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Cards must split evenly into groups; otherwise False immediately
How many cards of each value
Smallest value first: it can only start a group (nothing smaller is left to extend)
Not enough cards of value y to continue c groups
Uses c cards of each value of the c groups started at x
Processing all groups starting at x at once

bullets: All counts reach 0, so the answer is True: groups `[1,2,3] [2,3,4] [6,7,8]`.

blocks.h: Why start from the smallest card?
p: The smallest remaining card can only be the first card of its group (a group is consecutive, and nothing smaller remains). That forces the group `x, x+1, …, x+g−1`. Repeating the forced choice either finishes or finds a missing card.

bullets: Time: O(n log n) for sorting the distinct values.

846.takeaway: Greedy from the smallest card: it must start a group, so remove consecutive runs using counts.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Index of the first occupied seat
Index of the last occupied seat (reverse, find the first 1, convert back)
Edge gaps: sitting at seat 0 or n−1 gives the full gap length
Between two people, sitting in the middle gives half the gap (rounded down)

blocks.h: Why do the edges use the whole gap but the middle uses half?
p: At an edge there is only one neighbour, so the distance to it is the full gap. Between two people the closest neighbour is on either side, so the best seat is the middle, which is half the gap, rounded down.

bullets: Space: O(n) for the reversed copy (O(1) with an index scan).

849.takeaway: Check the two edge gaps in full and every inner gap in half.
